cim: How are local libraries adapting to artificial intelligence?
kihagyva: P3: 41 pont, tendencia 20%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: How are local libraries adapting to artificial intelligence?
szoveg_eredeti:
The rapid growth of artificial intelligence is changing how libraries globally operate and assist citizens, according to the American Library Association. Instead of viewing generative AI as a threat, librarians interviewed by The Cavalier Daily in the Charlottesville area are using it as a tool to access new services that help students navigate information while researching, studying or using library resources.

Within the University, the University Library worked with the College of Arts and Sciences in its creation of the AI Literacy and Action Lab. The lab, which was announced in April, aims to work with faculty to incorporate AI literacy into the University, and has hosted multiple speakers, according to Meridith Wolnick, director of teaching and learning and co-chair of the lab.

The lab utilizes the AI Literacy Framework created by University Dean of Libraries Leo Lo to guide its partnerships and classes regarding ethical use of AI, and Wolnick explained that the lab is planning to host more AI-related workshops throughout the school year.

Wolnick — who noted her perspective is not representative of the University Library system — said that with the increase of generative AI, librarians aim to keep their fundamental values the same — helping students understand information and eventually navigate it independently. Wolnick said she is especially interested in two AI tools called Consensus and LeapSpace, which are search appliances for academic articles.

“I'm not interested in discouraging students from using AI,” Wolnick said. “I want them to understand what they're doing when they use it. There are some wonderful opportunities to make research easier and more accessible, but students also need to recognize when using a tool might mean missing an opportunity to develop their own understanding.”

Libraries also offer specialized expertise that students cannot acquire through the use of an AI tool, Wolnick said. According to Wolnick, librarians are able to assist students in researching academic journals and articles.

Despite the ways in which AI can be useful in the library, Wolnick said that AI becomes a concern for librarians and students when information access is easy, but inaccurate. AI cannot always provide the context or necessary information students need, which may lead to an inability to distinguish what is accurate or what should be further investigated, Wolnick said.

“Learning to use specialized research tools can take more time and effort than simply asking AI a question,” Wolnick said. “But once you develop those skills, you have access to a much richer pool of resources and perspectives.”

Similarly, the Jefferson-Madison Regional Library that serves the broader Charlottesville community is also adapting to changing tools with the growth of AI, JMRL Library Director David Plunkett said in a statement to The Cavalier Daily.

JMRL has three library branches located in Charlottesville — Central Library, Gordon Avenue Library and Northside Library. According to Plunkett, with AI growth, JMRL continues to aim to connect people with each other and foster a community of research and learning in and around Charlottesville.

“If anything, AI reinforces many of the outstanding values of public libraries,” Plunkett said. “[It can help] people navigate any stream of information safely [and connect] them to the resources they need.”

Librarians have also had to do a lot of work behind the scenes in choosing what materials to make available to students, said Crystal Newell, senior director of library and academic support at Piedmont Virginia Community College. Newell said library collections are accumulated based on authority — whether the author has adequate expertise — currency and alignment with academic curriculum in the case of academic libraries. Newell is revising PVCC’s collection development and electronic resources policies to evaluate digital materials that either have AI built in, or were extensively written by AI.

“Libraries select collections based on criteria including authority … validity … and currency,” Newell said. “Users trust libraries to provide this authoritative information. Generative AI could undermine this trust if approached without careful consideration.”

While PVCC has not currently purchased any specific AI tools, they have enabled a natural language search AI tool in EBSCO, an interdisciplinary research database, Newell said. She also noted that she would like to see a “pause” on AI use in academia so students can develop necessary skills, like researching.

“Student voice is the most important part of learning,” Newell said. “Faculty and librarians do not want, or need, to hear what generative AI says, we could find that out ourselves. What matters is what the student brings to the process of research, that they ask themselves why this matters and what conclusion they can arrive at that furthers the conversation.”

Administrators from the University Library, JMRL and PVCC Library expressed confidence that AI will not replace human librarians nor undermine libraries’ fundamental values. Instead the administrators are focused on how AI can be integrated into the current library systems. AI cannot replace personal judgment, but it can enhance technology of the institutions, Plunkett emphasized.

“Librarians have always helped connect people to information, and to evaluate that information,” Plunkett said. “The tools have changed quite a bit over the years, but the fundamental need for a guiding hand from library staff in areas of information literacy has not.”

Anna Ivanov is a staffer on the news desk.
